questions.answer: The span is the set of all linear combinations of the listed vectors: \[\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf v_1,\ldots,\mathbf v_k\}=\{c_1\mathbf v_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf v_k:c_i\in\mathbb R\}.\] It contains every vector that can be built from the list.
Choose every coefficient equal to zero. Then \(0\mathbf v_1+\cdots+0\mathbf v_k=\mathbf0\). Therefore \(\mathbf0\) is always in the span, even if the listed vectors are not independent.
Every vector in the span has form \(t(2,0)=(2t,0)\). Since \(2t\) can be any real number, this is exactly the \(x\)-axis: \(\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb R\}\).
Yes. For any \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\), \((x,y)=x(1,0)+y(0,1)\). Since every target vector can be written as a linear combination of the two vectors, they span \(\mathbb R^2\).
We need \(t(1,2)=(3,4)\). The first component gives \(t=3\). The second component would then be \(2t=6\), not \(4\). No single \(t\) works, so \((3,4)\) is not in the span.
Solve \(t(1,2)=(3,6)\). Components give \(t=3\) and \(2t=6\), which are consistent. Hence \((3,6)=3(1,2)\), so \((3,6)\) lies in the span.

questions.prompt: Find coefficients showing that \((5,1)\) is in the span of \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\).

questions.answer: No. Any linear combination has form \(a(1,0,0)+b(0,1,0)=(a,b,0)\), whose third component is always \(0\). For example, \((0,0,1)\) cannot be produced. Therefore the pair does not span \(\mathbb R^3\).

questions.prompt: Show that \((1,0,1)\) and \((0,1,1)\) span the plane \(z=x+y\) in \(\mathbb R^3\).
questions.answer: A linear combination is \(a(1,0,1)+b(0,1,1)=(a,b,a+b)\), which satisfies \(z=x+y\). Conversely, any vector in the plane has form \((x,y,x+y)=x(1,0,1)+y(0,1,1)\). Therefore the two vectors span exactly that plane.

No. Both vectors lie on the same line because \((2,4)=2(1,2)\). Their linear combinations have form \(a(1,2)+b(2,4)=(a+2b)(1,2)\), still on that line. They cannot produce a vector such as \((1,0)\), so they do not span \(\mathbb R^2\).

Let \((x,y)\) be an arbitrary target. Solve \(a(1,0)+b(1,1)=(x,y)\). Components give \(a+b=x\) and \(b=y\). Thus \(b=y\) and \(a=x-y\). Since these coefficients exist for every \((x,y)\), the vectors span \(\mathbb R^2\).

questions.prompt: Adding a vector already in a span does not change the span. Illustrate using \((1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\).
questions.answer: Since \((1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1)\), the third vector is already in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\). Any combination \(a(1,0)+b(0,1)+c(1,1)\) equals \((a+c)(1,0)+(b+c)(0,1)\). So the span is still \(\mathbb R^2\), unchanged by adding \((1,1)\).

questions.prompt: For which \(k\) do \((1,1)\) and \((1,k)\) span \(\mathbb R^2\)?
questions.answer: They span \(\mathbb R^2\) exactly when they are not scalar multiples. Use determinant \(\begin{vmatrix}1&1\\1&k\end{vmatrix}=k-1\). The determinant is non-zero when \(k\ne1\). Therefore the pair spans \(\mathbb R^2\) for \(k\ne1\), and fails when \(k=1\).

questions.prompt: Find all \(a\) such that \((1,0,a),(0,1,a),(1,1,2a)\) span \(\mathbb R^3\).
questions.answer: The third vector is always the sum of the first two, since \((1,1,2a)=(1,0,a)+(0,1,a)\). Thus the span has at most two independent directions. A two-dimensional span cannot equal \(\mathbb R^3\). Therefore there is no real value of \(a\) for which the three vectors span \(\mathbb R^3\).

Use the column determinant \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&t\end{pmatrix}=t\). The vectors span \(\mathbb R^3\) exactly when this determinant is non-zero. Therefore they span \(\mathbb R^3\) for \(t\ne0\), and do not span it for \(t=0\).

The set spans \(\mathbb R^2\) if at least two vectors are not scalar multiples. If \(a\ne1\), then \((1,a)\) and \((1,1)\) are not scalar multiples, so the set spans. If \(a=1\), all three vectors equal \((1,1)\), so the span is only a line. Therefore the set spans \(\mathbb R^2\) exactly when \(a\ne1\).

Use the determinant \(\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\b&b&1\end{pmatrix}\). Expanding gives \(1(1-b)-0+1(0-b)=1-2b\). The columns span \(\mathbb R^3\) when \(1-2b\ne0\). Thus they span for \(b\ne\tfrac12\), and fail for \(b=\tfrac12\).

questions.prompt: A student says two vectors in \(\mathbb R^3\) can span all of \(\mathbb R^3\) if they are long enough. Explain the error.
questions.answer: Length does not determine how many independent directions a set provides. Linear combinations of two vectors use only two scalar coefficients, so their span is at most a plane through the origin. The vector lengths can be large, but the number of independent directions is still at most two. Therefore two vectors cannot span all of \(\mathbb R^3\).

questions.prompt: Prove that the span of any list of vectors is a subspace.
questions.answer: Let \(S=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf v_1,\ldots,\mathbf v_k\}\). The zero vector is in \(S\) by taking all coefficients zero. If \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\in S\), write \(\mathbf a=\sum_i r_i\mathbf v_i\) and \(\mathbf b=\sum_i s_i\mathbf v_i\). Then \(\lambda\mathbf a+\mu\mathbf b=\sum_i(\lambda r_i+\mu s_i)\mathbf v_i\), another linear combination of the same vectors. Hence \(S\) is a subspace.

Every vector in \(\operatorname{span}(T)\) is a linear combination of vectors from \(T\). Since every vector of \(T\) is also a vector of \(S\), the same linear combination is also a linear combination of vectors from \(S\). Therefore every vector in \(\operatorname{span}(T)\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}(S)\), so \(\operatorname{span}(T)\subseteq\operatorname{span}(S)\).
